title: Improvement of strength-ductility combination in ultra-high-strength medium-Mn Q&P steel by tailoring the characteristics of martensite/ retained austenite constituents
abstract: In this study, a low carbon medium-Mn steel was subjected to different quenching and partitioning (Q&P) processes to investigate fraction and morphology of fresh martensite and retained austenite constituents (M/RA) on microstructure characteristics and mechanical properties by EPMA, EBSD, TEM and tensile test, etc. By increasing the annealing time, the fraction of M/RA decreases, which gradually evolves from large-sized blocky islands to fine granular or lath-like shape in morphology. This is attributed to the larger-grained prior austenite and the uniform distribution of Mn which reduces the thermal stability of austenite and hence increases the volume fraction of tempered martensite (TM) as well as effectively refining the resultant microstructure. Furthermore, a new CCE-PAG model has been proposed by taking into account the effect of the prior austenite grain size. Compared with the traditional CCE model, the prediction of RA fraction increases first and then decreases with the annealing time, being in better agreement with the experimental results. The long-time annealed samples show a better combination of strength and ductility, i.e., their tensile strength reaches ultra-high 1312–1391 MPa, yield strength up to 730–765 MPa, and the elongation is higher than 16%, which results from the existence of large-fractioned TM structure and the sustained TRIP effect. In short-time annealed samples, the crack tends to be initiated and propagated at the edge of coarse M/RA islands, leading to the final brittle fracture.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Compared with traditional low-carbon steel, advanced high-strength steel (AHSS) has higher strength and better ductility. Therefore, its widely use can greatly reduce the weight of the vehicle body to save fossil energy consumption and reduce exhaust emissions [ 1 , 2 ]. As a representative of the third generation of AHSS, quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel and medium manganese (medium-Mn) steel achieve an excellent combination of strength and ductility by virtue of the TRIP effect of retained austenite (RA) [ 3–6 ], and therefore they have always been a research hotspot in academic and industrial fields [ 7–14 ]. However, in order to achieve higher strength, e.g., ultimate tensile strength (UTS) above 980 MPa, the low-carbon Q&P steel has to add expensive microalloying elements or introduce more amount of hard martensite, thus inevitably sacrificing the ductility to a certain extent [ 15–18 ]. Medium-Mn steel has an amazing combination of strength and ductility (i.e. the product of strength and elongation exceeding 30 GPa%), but its strength is often relatively low because of the lack of harder martensite phase [ 9 ]. More importantly, during stamping process, it also faces technical problems that are not beneficial for industrial application, such as long Lüders bands and serious serration behavior [ 19 ]. Consequently, it becomes very necessary to find a new way to obtain an excellent strength and ductility combination for ultrahigh-strength steels with relatively small alloying additions.

Some researchers try to take into account the advantages of the above two, so the Q&P process is applied to medium-Mn steel. In 2011, Moor E D et al. [ 20 ] took the lead in applying different Q&P processes to C–Mn–Si steels with 0.2–0.3 wt.% C and 3∼5 wt.% Mn. The results show that the samples subjected to Q&P treatment after full austenitizing can obtain higher volume fraction of tempered martensite and RA, leading to a concurrent increase in strength and ductility. Although this work did not fully clarify the relationship between the microstructure and mechanical properties, it greatly aroused people's attention to the Q&P steel with higher Mn addition. The results reported by Cho L et al. [ 21 ] indicate that refining the prior austenite grain size can accelerate the carbon partitioning kinetics, and finally the TWIP and TRIP effects simultaneously occur in small-grained samples, which significantly improves the mechanical properties. Furthermore, Hajyakbary et al. [ 22 ] analyzed the relationship between the yield strength and mechanical behavior of each phase, and revealed that in the medium-Mn Q&P steel, tempered martensite in which dislocation density increases with decreasing the quenching temperature, plays a determining role on the variation in yield strength.

Unfortunately, the martensite in the medium-Mn steel is prone to brittle fracture during tempering, and the extremely poor ductility limits the further application of this type of steel [ 23 , 24 ]. Kuzmina et al. [ 25 ] found that, compared with the effect of impurity elements, the segregation of Mn at the grain boundary possibly contributes to brittle fracture because of reducing the grain boundary cohesion of medium-Mn steel, but there are different explanations in related experiments [ 26 ]. Recently, some reports have pointed out that the size and type of martensite have a great influence on the mechanical properties of Q&P steel [ 27 , 28 ]. Actually, in order to reduce the rolling force or simulate the coiling process, the ART process needs to be used to soften the matrix before cold rolling, which will inevitably cause the Mn concentration gradient [ 29–31 ]. The homogenizing annealing will inevitably lead to the growth of prior austenite grain size, further affecting the characteristics of fresh martensite and retained austenite constituents (or so-called “M/RA”). On the other hand, as an austenite stabilizing element, Mn affects the subsequent phase transformation by affecting the thermal stability of prior austenite. In the early studies, most reports related the mechanical properties of Q&P steel to the volume fraction of RA, TRIP and TWIP effects, but there is still a lack of knowledge about the coupling effects of prior austenite grain size and Mn distribution on the MA characteristics and mechanical behaviors in medium-Mn Q&P steel.

In the current work, a novel microstructure design involving alloying and Q&P processing has been adopted to obtain a better strength-ductility combination in ultra-high-strength steels, and to provide insights into the effects of prior austenite grain size and Mn distribution on M/RA constituents and mechanical properties. In particular, it focuses on the relationship between the volume fraction change of M/RA and the morphological evolution of RA, as well as fracture characteristics during tensile testing. At the same time, the crystallographic characteristics of retained austenite and martensite variants are obtained and analyzed by EBSD technology.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of the investigated low-carbon medium-Mn steel is Fe-0.2C-5.05Mn-1.56Si (wt.%). The rectangular ingot (100 mm∗100 mm∗80 mm) was homogenized at 1200 °C for 3 h, and hot rolled to 5 mm thickness with the finish-rolling temperature of 930 °C, followed by air cooling. Then take a sample from the hot rolled sheet to measure the important phase transition temperature by a dilatometer. The A C1  and A C3  temperatures were 605 °C and 775 °C, respectively. In order to reduce the rolling force, according to our previous research, it is necessary to anneal at 650 °C for 3 h before cold rolling. Subsequently, the plate was cold-rolled to about 1.2 mm with a reduction of 76%. Tensile specimens were machined from the cold-rolled sheet along the rolling direction with dimensions of 25 mm gauge length and 12.5 mm width. The annealing treatments presented in  Fig. 1 
                       were carried out in a tube resistance furnace and salt baths. The specimens were firstly austenitized at 780 °C for different time (180s, 300s, 600s, 1800s, 3600s), then quenched to 150 °C which was determined by CCE model to obtain maximum amount of RA, and reheated to 450 °C for 300s followed by water quenching. The Q&P samples were referred to as QP-180/300/6001800/3600. In order to characterize the degree of austenitization, a series of as-quenched processes were designed, which were held at 780 °C for different time followed by water quenching. Hereafter, the as-quenched samples were referred to as DQ-180/300/600/1800/3600, respectively. In order to reveal the prior austenite grain boundaries, the corresponding samples were etched in a filtered saturated solution consisting of 5wt.% C 6 H 3 N 3 O 7  and 95wt.% H 2 O for 30s at 70 °C。The mechanical properties of the specimens were measured by the Instron 100 kN tensile testing machine at room temperature. The resulting microstructures and fracture morphology were characterized by Ultra 55 field emission Scanning electron microscope (SEM). In order to make a qualitative analysis of element distribution, line and plane scanning was performed by using JEOL JXA-8530 F Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) equipped with Wavelength dispersive spectrometer (WDS). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) samples were obtained by punching holes in the same area of the SEM and EBSD samples. After manual grinding to a thickness of 45 μm, it was thinned by double-jet in a 10 vol% perchlorate alcohol solution at −25 °C with operating voltage of 32 V. In addition, the analysis of Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) was applied to typical samples with the voltage of 20 kV and a step size of 0.05 μm. The retained austenite fraction and its carbon content were measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation operated at 40 kV and 100 mA at room temperature, and the samples were scanned from 40° to 120° at a scanning rate of 2°/min. Before EBSD and XRD detection, all samples were prepared by electrochemical polishing (25 V for 26s in a mixed solution of 87.5 vol% ethanol and 12.5 vol% perchloric acid). sections.heading: Microstructural and elements distribution characterization
paragraphs:
The optical microscope images of DQ samples for different austenitization time are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         , which present the degree of austenitization and prior austenite grain size. Etched by saturated picric acid solution, the prior austenite grain boundaries can be identified. As shown in  Fig. 2 f, the size of prior austenite increases approximately from 0.4 μm to 21 μm, as the annealing time is prolonged from 180s to 3600s, which is measured by the line-intercept method.

Figure 3 
                          shows the corresponding microstructures of samples after different annealing times. It is clear that for all samples, the final microstructures are composed of initial martensite (i.e., tempered martensite, TM), fresh martensite (M) and retained austenite (RA), or so-called M/RA constituents. The tempered martensite, which formed during the first quenching followed by tempering during the partitioning step, has a rough structure with internally etched features and shows gray background. It should be noticed that some fine carbide particles are observed inside TM ( Fig. 3 d and e), which is the product of martensite tempering. As compared with DQ samples, the microstructure after Q&P processing is significantly subdivided and refined due to the formation of initial martensite during the first quenching. Subsequently, some austenite is transformed into M/RA during final quenching process, which are characterized by island structure with a bright edge. In general, there are two kinds of morphologies for different treatments. As compared with QP-180, QP-300 and QP-600 samples ( Fig. 3 a, b, c), the microstructures of QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples ( Fig. 3 d, e) are more homogeneous and fibrous.  Figure 3 f is a statistical diagram of the M/RA volume fraction for different processes. It can be clearly seen that the fraction of M/RA has a negative correlation with annealing time. In the cases of QP-180, QP-300 and QP-600 samples, the microstructures mainly consist of blocky M/RA islands and minor amount of needle-like M/RA or RA. However, there is few existence of large-sized blocky M/RA but increasing fraction of needle-like M/RA in QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples, which means that the extension of annealing time can dramatically affect matrix microstructure evolution from blocky shape to long needle-like structure. Note that, although the volume fraction of blocky M/RA in QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples is very small, it still exists.

On the other hand, the characteristics of carbon and manganese distributions in different Q&P treatments was revealed by WDS technique, as shown in  Fig. 4 
                         . It is clear that the TM is usually carbon-depleted. Whilst the edge of M/RA adjacent to TM is carbon-enriched, the central area is carbon-depleted, e.g., the area indicated by the red arrow ( Fig. 4 a2 and 4b2). On the whole, the QP-3600 sample having elevated fractions of TM and needle-like M/RA structures within them achieves a better C partitioning effect than the QP-180 sample in which carbon is mostly enriched at the edge of the large-sized M/RA block. Hence, compared with blocky M/RA, TM has an enhanced ability of carbon partitioning, which is more helpful to stable RA. Notably, the Mn distribution in the QP-180 is apparently non-uniform, which is related to the low diffusion coefficient of Mn during annealing [ 33 ], but as the annealing time increases, this phenomenon can be minimized in the QP-3600 sample. It should be pointed out that the Mn-enriched area usually corresponds to the M/RA island, as shown by the yellow arrows in  Fig. 4 . This phenomenon mostly occurs in the QP-180 sample with non-uniform distribution of Mn, but in QP-3600 sample with the uniform distribution of Mn, the microstructure of blocky M/RA is gradually replaced by the needle-like structure in TM.

sections.heading: Characterization of retained austenite morphology by EBSD
paragraphs:
Besides, EBSD technology is also used to characterize RA finely. For QP-300, as indicated by the black circle in  Fig. 5 
                         a, the RA with a micron-sized blocky morphology is mainly located at the PAGBs or triple junctions. As for QP-600, RA undergoes a relatively large change in the morphology and size. Likewise, most of the blocky RA exists at the PAGBs or triple junctions. However, as indicated by the black arrow in  Fig. 5 b, the size of the RA is greatly reduced, and a large amount of fine granular RA appears in the microstructure. In particular, nano-scale lath or needle-like RA between the TM (indicated by the black arrow) can be observed in QP-1800. It can be seen that the morphology and size of RA are strongly dependent on the annealing time.  Figure 5 d shows the distribution of RA size corresponding to different annealing processes. It can be clearly seen that as the annealing time increases, the RA size gradually decreases. For QP-1800 samples, all of RA grains are smaller than 1 μm in diameter, and most of them are in the range of 0∼0.2 μm, accounting for about 60% of the total. However, for QP-300 sample, the RA with a diameter less than 1 μm accounts for only 33%, and the large-sized particles more than 1 μm account for 10% of the total.

sections.heading: Comparison of mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The engineering stress–strain curves of samples with different heat treatments are plotted in  Fig. 7 
                            a,b, and the corresponding mechanical properties are presented in  Fig. 7 c,d and  Table 2 
                            . As shown in  Fig. 7 a, the stress–strain curve of QP-180∼QP-600 samples show continuous yielding characteristics. The absence of yield point elongation is frequently attributed to higher density of mobile dislocations present in materials. In contrast, QP-1800 and QP-3600 are featured by discontinuous yielding behavior, and enlarged views of yielding presented in  Fig. 7 b,c clearly show that with the increase of annealing time, yield strength (YS) continues to increase from 730 MPa to 1066 MPa, where QP-180 has the lowest YS of 730 MPa, and QP-3600 has the highest YS of 1066 MPa. Therefore, compared with QP-1800/3600, QP-180∼QP-600 all show higher ultimate tensile strength (UTS) values (>1407 MPa). Clearly, all samples exhibit ultra-high UTS (>1300 MPa), and the highest UTS (1545 MPa) is obtained in QP-600. It can be seen from  Fig. 7 d that total elongation (TEL) and product of strength and elongation (PSE) both gradually increase as the annealing time increases. Meanwhile, QP-180 and QP-300 have the poorest ductility, showing brittle fracture. But QP-1800/3600 perform similarly, and both of them have the best strength-ductility balance, and the PSE value is about 22.4 GPa%.

sections.heading: Fracture characterization
paragraphs: During the tensile test, it can be found that the medium-Mn Q&P steel often suffered from brittle fracture or poor elongation (brittle fracture occurs in QP-180/QP-300, and the elongation of QP-600 is only 11%). Therefore, in order to analyze the relevant low-energy fracture mechanism, SEM is used to characterize the crack types of different treatment processes in this section.

As shown in  Fig. 8 
                            , the fracture morphologies of different samples after tensile tests are displayed. The enlarged pictures are corresponding to the red rectangle areas. It is apparent that when austenitization time is less than 600s, the fracture propagates mainly along the grain boundaries, exhibiting rock sugar-like notches, while only a small number of dimples appear. Additionally, as shown by the yellow arrows in  Fig. 8 b, a large number of secondary micro-cracks are found in the fracture area, and some micro-cracks combine with each other through grain boundaries to form long cracks, which is known as intergranular fracture [ 26 ]. Its appearance means that the grain boundary binding force is weak, which will become an easy crack propagation path, a kind of low-energy failure mode. This result comes to accord with the poor elongation in the experimental  Fig. 7 a. It is worth noting that QP-1800 ( Fig. 8 c) shows both ductile and brittle fracture, which can be clearly divided into two different regions: ductile region 1 at the center of the fracture, and brittle regions 2 at the edges of fracture.  Figure 8 c1 is the enlarged view of region 1, and it can be seen that there are a large number of dimples with non-uniform size. Moreover, as the distance from the center increases, the size of the large dimples increases. Generally speaking, small and uniform dimples mean that the sample has good plasticity [ 34 ]. However, region 2 is dominated by intergranular fracture ( Fig. 8c2 ). So, it can be inferred that QP-1800 exhibits a mixed fracture mode in which the ductile fracture is dominant, thus more energy can be absorbed during fracture, matching its good plasticity. As for QP-3600, the presence of a large number of small dimples reveals a pronounced ductile fracture characteristic ( Fig. 8 d, e).

As seen in  Fig. 9 d, the RA volume fraction calculated by the CCE model is a constant (∼20.3%), which shows a great difference from the XRD detection. In contrast, the RA content obtained by the CCE-PAG model shows a trend of rising first and then falling with annealing time, which is consistent with the measured results. The reasonable explanation for this trend is that austenite with smaller grain size has higher thermal stability, resulting in lower M 1s  temperature, so only a small amount of TM can be obtained after the initial quenching. Consequently, during the partitioning stage, they cannot provide sufficient carbon atoms to stabilize untransformed austenite, thereby leading to larger amount of M/RA in the resultant microstructure.

Although the results predicted by the CCE-PAG model are more reasonable and closer to the experimental values, there is a certain deviation between these calculations and actual results. Especially, the actual values of QP-180 and QP-300 samples are higher than the predicted RA values. The QP-300 sample has the maximum measured value of RA, while this theoretical prediction corresponds to the QP-600 sample. Combined with the WDS results in  Fig. 4 , it can be seen that there is a large variation in the concentration distribution of Mn for the samples annealed for different times. In addition, the microstructure in the Mn-enriched region usually corresponds to blocky M/RA islands, which is similar to previous studies [ 40 ]. In fact, as an austenite stabilizing element, the enrichment of Mn will result in a drop in the Ms temperature. It is not difficult to conclude that in the Mn-enriched region, the fraction of TM will be further reduced during the initial quenching process, so the untransformed austenite content increases and largely transforms into blocky M/RA during the final quenching process. For QP-600/1800/3600 samples, the actual RA contents are generally lower than the results given by the CCE-PAG model. It is likely attributed to the pinning effect of dislocations and defects on the carbon, which cause the loss of carbon atoms during the partitioning process [ 41 ]. In order to further understand the relationship between concentration gradient of Mn and annealing time, typical samples are analyzed by line canning technology of EPMA.

As shown in  Fig. 10 
                         a, there is an obvious non-uniform distribution of Mn in the QP-180 sample, and its maximum deviation from the bulk concentration (5.05 wt.%) is approximately 1.3%. In contrast, Mn distribution in QP-600 sample gradually becomes uniform and approaches the bulk concentration ( Fig. 10 c). As for QP-3600, the non-uniform distribution of Mn in the austenite is remarkably reduced ( Fig. 10 d), and the maximum deviation from the bulk concentration is less than 0.5 wt.%.  Formula (11)  is used to quantitatively show the deviation of the Mn content from the bulk concentration and the detailed data is given in  Table 4 
                         . It can be seen from  Table 4  that the non-uniform distribution of Mn begins to weaken gradually as the annealing time is more than 600s, and QP-600 and QP-1800 samples have the same degree of deviation (although it is not shown in  Fig. 10 ). Clearly, the non-uniform distribution of Mn only exists in samples annealed for a short time, such as QP-180 and QP-300. Once the annealing time is further extended (annealing time exceeds 600s), this phenomenon will be weakened.

sections.heading: Characterization and evolution analysis of microstructure
paragraphs:
Owing to the spatial resolution limitations of EBSD, finer nanoscale M/RA (width <50 nm) has not been characterized. In order to further analyze more details of the microstructure, TEM characterization is performed on typical samples. In the QP-180 ( Fig. 11 
                         a), it can be clearly seen that, in addition to the carbon-depleted lath martensite ( Fig. 11 b), the carbon-enriched twin martensite structures are also observed ( Fig. 11 a). Generally, it is believed that the former corresponds to TM formed by tempering during the partitioning process, and the latter corresponds to M generated from untransformed austenite with higher C content in the final quenching process. The increased fraction of M also means that the ideal C partitioning does not occur. Note that, there are many dislocation tangles around M in QP-180 ( Fig. 11 a). By using the dark-field image, it can be seen that there are a large number of micron-sized blocky RA near the grain boundaries in QP-180 ( Fig. 11 c), whose size is approximately 0.1–1.5 μm. Compared to QP-180, the RA of QP-3600 mainly appears a lath shape ( Fig. 11 f), which is located between the martensite lath, with a size of 50–100 nm. Many previous studies have shown that the shape and size of RA in the Q&P steel play a remarkable role in mechanical properties. The lath RA is widely considered to have excellent thermodynamic and mechanical stability; thus the TRIP effect can continue working during deformation, which play a remarkable role on the resulting mechanical properties. Whilst, using the SAED (selected area electron diffraction) technology, it can be found that the RA in QP-3600 and the adjacent martensite lath have a coherent orientation relationship ( Fig. 11 f): (

Additionally, some martensite laths are curved, which may be related to the interface migration during the partitioning process. Based on further comparison of 15 TEM images for each process, it can be seen that with increasing the annealing time, the morphology and size of RA or martensite vary significantly, i.e., twin martensite is gradually changed into lathy martensite, and blocky M/RA is replaced by lath RA.

Although the detailed analysis of TEM maps provides the evolution law of RA, it cannot be ignored that there are still some granular M/RA in the QP-1800 sample ( Fig. 5 c). In order to further study the crystallographic relationship between different RA and adjacent martensite, the QP-1800 sample in  Fig. 5 c is analyzed in detail, and the corresponding enlarged view is shown in  Fig. 12 
                         . As shown in  Fig. 12 a, the prior austenite is mostly transformed into martensite, except that minor amounts of austenite with the same orientation as parent phase is still retained. By using the ARPGE software, the parent austenite can be reconstructed [ 42 ]. Besides, the pattern of the KS OR has a high degree of symmetry on the {001} pole figure. Hence, combining the above conditions, the prior austenite can be identified. As shown in  Fig. 12 b, the three Bain zones indicated by the gray arrows are 90° apart on the great circles, which indicates that the highlight region in  Fig. 12 a belongs to the same prior austenite [ 43 ].

Due to the symmetry of cubic crystals, when the KS OR is satisfied, the prior austenite will produce 24 possible equivalent crystallographic orientations, i.e., martensitic variants (denoted as V1–V24). Here, in order to analyze martensite variants in detail, V1 is defined as austenite (111)γ plane and [

The relevant calculations are discussed in detail in ref. [ 44 ]. By rotating the {001} pole figure which is obtained from the experimental data until it coincides with the standard {001} pole figure, and the 24 variants obtained from the experiment can be plotted.

The martensite variants information is shown in  Fig. 12 c. It can be revealed that during the phase transformation, not all variants appear, which means that natural variant selection has worked. Generally speaking, the selection phenomenon of martensitic variants is mainly due to the limited phase change space. Meanwhile, V21&V24, V13&V16, V14&V17, V18&V15 and V10&V7 have been observed as special variants combination with the minimum misorientation (10.53°), which is also called sub-block. Usually, this phenomenon is explained by the coordinated martensitic transformation stress [ 44 ]. Furthermore, it can be found that granular RA mainly exists at the interface of PAGB, packet and block. It is worth noting that in the upper half of the prior austenite, there is coarsened variants (V14&V17) and only a small amount of RA. So far, it is generally believed that the coarse variant forms in the early stage of martensite transformation as a result of the sequence of martensite transformation [ 45 ]. And the coarse variant has better plasticity and is easy to occur in austenite with lower stability [ 46 ]. On the contrary, the variants in the lower half are greatly refined in size and become more complex in distribution, and simultaneously the granular RA increases in volume fraction. These variants significantly increase the packet and block interfaces, which can also be verified from the lower BC value of the corresponding area in  Fig. 12 a. Therefore, the increased fraction of interfaces will provide more paths for C partitioning, so a large amount of granular RA can be finally retained. Hence, it is reasonable to conclude that the morphology and size of RA are strongly related to different treatments.

As stated above, the general features of microstructural evolution can be summarized and schematically shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . For the medium-Mn Q&P steel, the microstructural characteristics such as fraction, size and morphology of the constituent phases, considerably depends on the prior austenite grain size and the distribution of Mn atoms. For short-time annealed samples, the small grain size and non-uniform distribution of Mn lead to the relatively higher thermal stability of austenite. Thus, after the initial quenching (QT = 150°C), only a minor fraction of TM can be formed and a large amount of untransformed austenite will easily transform into blocky M/RA islands during the final quenching, and the RA predominantly in blocky morphology exists at the PAGB and triple junctions. As the annealing time increases, the prior austenite grain size rapidly increases, the Mn concentration gradient in austenite is gradually eliminated and its distribution become more uniform. Compared with the fine-grained samples, larger amounts of TM form when it is quenched at the same QT. The RA is mainly located at the boundaries of lath-like or blocky M/RA, or between the TM laths. Thereby, the resulting microstructure is composed of TM and a small fraction of fine M/RA.

sections.heading: Comparison and analysis of mechanical properties and work hardening behavior
paragraphs:
It can be seen from  Fig. 7  that although the QP-180∼QP-600 samples exhibit higher UTS, their YS and TELs are extremely low. The UTS of QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples decreases slightly, but YS and TEL are greatly improved, so they have a better PSE value. Related studies [ 22 ] have shown that the YS will be positively correlated with the content of tempered martensite TM. Therefore, the increase of YS is attributed to the increase of the TM content in the microstructure with increasing the annealing time. For short-time annealed samples, their microstructures contain a large number of hard M/RA particles, so exhibiting higher UTS. Instead, the increasing fraction of TM leads to the decrease of UTS on prolonged annealing. The work hardening behavior of different samples is presented in  Fig. 14 
                         , and the change of instantaneous work hardening exponent with strain can be roughly divided into three stages: as the true strain increases, the exponent decays rapidly (stage 1), then it gradually rises accompanied by obvious serrations (stage 2), and finally decreases slowly with slight fluctuations (stage 3). It is generally believed that when the true strain increases, the dislocation slip in the martensite is responsible for the significant decrease in the exponent (stage 1). As the true strain continues to increase, the strain-induced RA to martensite transformation in the structure will be triggered which will delay the occurrence of necking and increase the work hardening ability (as shown in  Fig. 14 b, the steep peak caused by the TRIP effect can be clearly observed). In addition, some RA with low stability will preferentially transform into martensite [ 47 ], so this stage can be used to evaluate the stability of RA. As for stage 3, the coordinated deformation of multiple phases causes the exponent to drop, and more stable RA also begins to transform, so the curve is accompanied by slight fluctuations.

It can be clearly seen that there are large differences in work hardening ability of different samples. As shown in  Fig. 14 a, when the true strain is smaller than 0.02, the hardening exponents of QP-180 and QP-300 are much higher than other samples, exhibiting a large fluctuation on the curve of work hardening exponent plotted against true strain. This phenomenon is likely attributed to the presence of more mobile dislocations and the resultant accelerated recovery caused by higher fraction of coarse M/RA occurred in QP-180 and QP-300 samples. Likewise, compared with QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples, the QP-600 maintains a higher hardening exponent in the initial stage. Moreover, as the true strain continues to increase (>0.02), both the microstructural feature of M/RA (morphology, size, and distribution, etc) and TRIP effect of RA jointly play an important role in the deformation behaviors of medium-Mn Q&P steel. Based on the characterization results of EBSD and TEM, it can be found that the M/RA structures in the QP-180, QP-300 and QP600 are mainly large-sized blocky shape, and particularly the RA is considered to be poor in stability, so they are believed to be largely responsible for the relatively lower ductility of material. In QP-1800 and QP3600 samples, however, the M/RA and RA structures can be finely dispersed in the matrix with predominant tempered martensite, which leads to better stress/strain partitioning and sustained TRIP effect, thus providing the higher work hardening ability and excellent mechanical properties for the samples. Of course, it is seemingly reasonable that all of these are essentially determined by the grain size and Mn distribution of prior austenite.

sections.heading: Analysis of M/RA and crack propagation path
paragraphs:
Figure 15a∼ c show the band contrast (BC) maps of QP-300, QP-600 and QP-1800 samples with IPF-Z maps of RA, respectively. Usually, BC value is used to evaluate the internal dislocation density. Here, a lower BC value corresponds to M or M/RA, while a higher BC value represents TM. Compared with QP-600 and QP-1800 samples, the BC value of the QP-300 sample is the lowest. In addition to this, as shown in  Fig. 15d∼ f, Image Quality (IQ) maps are used to quantitatively reflect the energy storage of grains with lower BC value in the rectangular frame. The higher the IQ value, the better the quality of the diffraction pattern, which means that there are fewer lattice defects and stresses inside the grain [ 48 ]. It can be seen that the ranges of IQ value are 63–86 for QP-300 and 10–84 for QP-600, respectively. As for the QP-1800 sample, the grains of prior austenite have grown significantly, and the IQ value of resulting microstructure is increased to 83–103. It should be noted that the BC or IQ value cannot be used directly as the evidence to distinguish TM from M, because the grain boundary will also reduce them. According to reports [ 49 ], due to the relatively high C content, M usually corresponds to a typical misorientation angle about 55°.  Figure 15 
                         g and  Fig. 15 h respectively show the point-to-point misorientation analysis of the low IQ area indicated by the white rectangular in  Fig.15a  and  Fig.15c  along the direction of arrow AB. Compared with  Fig.15h ,  Fig.15g  clearly shows that there is a dense ∼55° misorientation angle, and the distance between them is less than 0.5 μm, which proves a large amount of M in the short-time annealed samples. This result is in accordance with the real evolution of the microstructure in  Fig. 3 .

Crack propagation paths near the fracture along the tensile direction in different samples are compared by SEM.  Figure 16 
                          shows the typical crack propagation of QP-180 and QP-3600, respectively. From red dotted straight line in  Fig. 16 a, it can be seen that the crack propagation path in QP-180 is relatively straight, and there are large blocky M/RA structures in the vicinity of the straight crack path. However, the crack propagation path in  Fig. 16 b is rather messy, indicating that more energy can be absorbed during the crack propagation, and there are no more M/RA islands around the crack, which is replaced by needle-like tempered martensite structure.

It is well known that the formation of cracks is the result of shear stress during tensile testing. Combined with Kernel average misorientation (KAM) results, dislocation density and defects on the grain boundaries of different samples can be known qualitatively [ 50 ]. The higher proportion of yellow-orange particles at grain boundaries in the QP-300 ( Fig. 17 
                         a) and QP-600 ( Fig. 17 c) samples indicates that more sub-grain boundaries and dislocation walls have been generated. These areas are also considered to be the origin of cracks during deformation, which have an adverse effect on mechanical properties [ 27 ]. In contrast, for QP-1800 sample, blue particles with lower KAM values occupy a larger proportion ( Fig. 17 d). Moreover, the areas are analyzed, which may contain more M or M/RA in  Fig. 17 a, as shown in  Fig. 17 b. The dark red area in the figure has a lower BC value, which corresponds to M with severe lattice distortion, while the light red area corresponds to TM, which is the blue area in the KAM map. It can be seen that the KAM value around M is significantly higher (as indicated by the white arrows). According to related literatures [ 51 ], coarse M/RA, especially when adjacent to the surrounding tempered martensite TM, is likely to cause early strain concentration, and this strain heterogeneity is likely to cause micro-cracks. This explains why M/RA islands are always observed around cracks in short-time annealed samples. Whilst, crack growth is hindered by grain boundaries, resulting in stress concentration, hence the secondary cracks ( Fig. 8 b) will appear to reduce stress. At the same time, the grain boundaries and interior of the RA adjacent to the M (as indicated by the yellow arrows) also have a higher KAM value. This is caused by the extrusion of M formation on the phase interface during the final quenching. As shown in  Fig. 17 e, although the fitting shapes of the KAM values of each sample are roughly same, as the f TM  increases, the curve is obviously shift to left, which has a low local misorientation (μ = 0.513 vs. μ = 0.472 vs. μ = 0.452). Based on the analysis of the SEM, the high KAM value in the QP-300 and QP-600 samples can be ascribed to the generation of a large number of M/RA during final quenching. Therefore, when shear stress is applied, the micro-cracks will preferentially occur at the grain boundary of short-time annealed samples, and finally it will lead to failure.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this work, a new ultra-high-strength medium-Mn steel has been designed by tailoring prior austenite size, Mn concentration distribution and final M/RA characteristics, and the relationship between the microstructure and mechanical properties was clarified. The main findings and conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            The resulting microstructure of medium-Mn Q&P steel, consisting of tempered martensite (TM), martensite/retained austenite (M/RA), is largely dependent on the prior austenite grain size and the distribution of Mn atoms. As the annealing time increases, the coarsening of prior austenite and the uniform distribution of Mn lead to an increase in TM content and a decrease in M/RA content by affecting austenite thermal stability and carbon partitioning behavior. Correspondingly, the predominant second-phase structure gradually evolve from large-sized blocky M/RA islands to relatively fine needle-like and granular morphology. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            A new CCE-PAG model has been proposed by considering the effect of prior austenite grain size on Ms temperature, which is in good agreement with the experimental values. When the quenching temperature is fixed, with increasing the annealing time, the RA volume fraction calculated by the CCE-PAG model firstly increases and then decreases, suggesting that the prior austenite grain size may play a more important role on the retention of RA, while the amount of RA calculated by traditional CCE model remains constant. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The excellent strength-ductility combination (UTS of 1312–1391 MPa, TEL of 16–17%, YS of 1011–1066 MPa) in the QP-1800 and QP-3600 samples have been achieved, which can be mostly attributed to the joint effects of the better deformation capability of large-fractioned TM structure and the sustained TRIP effect caused by fine and stable RA particles. Instead, the QP-180∼QP-600 samples with fine prior austenite grain size exhibit higher UTS (1407–1545 MPa), poor ductility (TEL of 3.3–11%) and lower YS (730–765 MPa) due to an increased amount of large-sized M/RA particles and the lack of TM. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The M/RA islands in the QP-180∼QP-600 samples usually correspond to the Mn-enriched area, and some locations even reaches 6.03 wt.%, while the Mn level in the ferritic matrix is close to the bulk concentration (5.05 wt.%), which may be associated with the non-uniform distribution of Mn after short time annealing. These coarse and hard structures effectively promoted the initiation and propagation of cracks along their edges in an approximate straight path, thereby severely deteriorating the ductility. The transition characteristics from brittle to ductile in fracture morphology was observed by increasing the volume fraction of TM
